title: Question kinds by where the answer lives
statement: Sort reading questions by where the answer lives, in one sentence, across several or with the reader's knowledge, and teach them in that order, each mastered before the next.
example: One design unlocks the 3 kinds strictly in that order and keeps kinds already mastered in the practice mix.
detail: An IES video on asking and answering questions, quoted in a reading course's review standard, sorts text-dependent questions into three kinds: right there, answered in one sentence; think and search, put together across several sentences; and author and me, which joins the text to the reader's own experience or learning and is also called inferential (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/teaching-moves/qar-evidence-source-taxonomy.md`). It recommends starting with right-there questions, moving on only once students show mastery of each kind, and having students find and highlight the supporting sentences. The standard's design tags every item with its kind, unlocks the kinds in that order while mastered kinds stay in the mix, and accepts no answer without the highlighted evidence. It is classroom guidance from a video, not a trial.

evidence.quote: When we teach students to answer questions, we should start with right there questions, then move to think and search questions, and finally author and me questions. Students should demonstrate mastery of each question type before they move to the next.
The simplest questions are right there questions — a type of text-dependent question for which the answer is stated in one sentence of the text.
This type of question is still text-dependent, but to answer it, a reader must put multiple pieces of information together across several sentences.
They require the reader to connect information in the text they have just read to their own prior experience or learning. Author and me questions are also known as inferential questions.
Find these sentences from the text. And when you find them, I want you to highlight them.
The mastery graph unlocks them strictly in that order
but previously-mastered types keep appearing in the mix (spaced practice) rather than disappearing
the answer cannot be submitted with an empty citation
